knowledge_point.title: Integrating a Reciprocal Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $-24$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{24}{x}\,\text{d}x & =-24\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\ & =-24\ln|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=-24\ln K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-24\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{24}{x}\,\text{d}x & =-24\ln|x|+C \\ & =-24\ln|x|+(-24)\ln K \\ & =-24(\ln|x|+\ln K) \\ & =-24\ln(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

We separate the integrand into the sum of two fractions so that we can simplify each term. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{18x-1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{18x}{x}-\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (18-\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =18\int \,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =18x-\ln|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=-\ln K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{18x-1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =18x-\ln|x|+C \\  & =18x-\ln|x|-\ln K \\  & =18x-(\ln|x|+\ln K) \\  & =18x-\ln(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $\frac{3}{2}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{2x}\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\ln|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=\frac{3}{2}\ln K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $\frac{3}{2}\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{2x}\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{2}\ln|x|+\frac{3}{2}\ln K \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(\ln|x|+\ln K) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\ln(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $\frac{13}{2}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{13}{2x}\text{d}x & =\frac{13}{2}\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{13}{2}\ln|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=\frac{13}{2}\ln K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $\frac{13}{2}\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{13}{2x}\text{d}x & =\frac{13}{2}\ln|x|+\frac{13}{2}\ln K \\  & =\frac{13}{2}(\ln|x|+\ln K) \\  & =\frac{13}{2}\ln(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating a Reciprocal Function and Simplifying the Arbitrary Constant Using the Laws of Logarithms

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $18$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 18{x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x & =18\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =18\ln|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=18\ln K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $18\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 18{x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x & =18\ln|x|+18\ln K \\  & =18(\ln|x|+\ln K) \\  & =18\ln(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

We separate the integrand into the sum of two fractions so that we can simplify each term. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7 + 11x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{7}{x}+\frac{11x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int (\frac{7}{x}+11)\,\text{d}x \\ & =7\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+11\int \,\text{d}x \\ & =7\ln|x|+11x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=7\ln K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $7\ln|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7 + 11x}{x}\,\text{d}x & =7\ln|x|+11x+C \\ & =7\ln|x|+11x+7\ln K \\ & =7\ln(K|x|)+11x.\end{aligned}
$$
